name: Aristotelianism
summary: Aristotelianism, as its political implications are drawn from Aristotle, holds that humans are naturally political animals and that the state exists for the good life, meaning virtuous activity, not mere survival. Regimes are judged by whether they serve the common good, with a mixed constitution and a large middle class the practical best, private property with shared use, limited wealth-getting, and law and public education shaping citizens' character. It accepts natural hierarchy of rulers and ruled, which modern adherents often reject in part.
scope: Aristotle's own ethics and politics (Nicomachean Ethics, Politics) as presented by the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy and the text of the Politics, with the later tradition (Aquinas, neo-Aristotelians such as MacIntyre) only in the background. Modern policy questions are mostly inferences and marked low confidence; his defence of natural slavery and male rule is recorded as his position, though many modern Aristotelians reject it.

keyFigures.name: Aristotle
keyFigures.role: Founder of the Peripatetic school and author of the Politics and Nicomachean Ethics

keyFigures.name: Thomas Aquinas
keyFigures.role: Medieval theologian who systematized Aristotle in line with Catholic theology

keyFigures.name: Alasdair MacIntyre
keyFigures.role: Neo-Aristotelian who revived virtue ethics in After Virtue

sources.usedFor: The later tradition, Aquinas, MacIntyre and virtue ethics.

universal-healthcare.rationale: Aristotle never discusses health provision; the state exists for the good life, but nothing says whether it should fund medical care, so this is an unresolved inference.

raise-minimum-wage.rationale: Wage-setting is never addressed; Aristotle wants moderate property and distrusts legislating equality, so a substantial statutory rise is not a natural fit.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: Aristotle treats unbounded exchange for profit as unnatural and subordinates wealth-getting to the good life, so he would not credit markets with allocating better than political judgment.

public-ownership.rationale: He argues against common ownership because people neglect what is held in common, favouring private property with common use.

tax-the-wealthy.rationale: Taxation levels are not a principled topic for him; he wants moderate wealth and warns that rich-poor extremes breed faction, but gives no tax doctrine.

unions-good.rationale: Unions did not exist; his concern for the common good and a stable middle class cuts both ways on organized labor, and the question stays unresolved.

property-fundamental.rationale: He defends private property against Plato but as a means to virtue and generosity, with use made common; he never treats it as an inviolable right to be hard to override.

regulate-corporations.rationale: Inferred from his view that wealth-getting must be limited by the good life and that the lawgiver shapes economic life; corporations as such are anachronistic.

cut-welfare.rationale: Inferred: he holds that poverty breeds faction and that the community should care for citizens' material means, so he would not favour cutting support as a principle.

worker-ownership.rationale: He excludes laborers from full citizenship and never proposes worker ownership; inferred from his preference for ownership by virtuous, leisured citizens.

surveillance-ok.rationale: Not addressed; adherents would weigh security against liberty by practical judgment, with no settled doctrine.

legalize-drugs.rationale: Inferred from the lawgiver's task of cultivating virtue and moderation in citizens, which makes permissive drug policy a poor fit.

restrict-hate-speech.rationale: Not addressed; the lawgiver shapes character but Aristotle gives no speech doctrine, and adherents divide.

strong-leader.rationale: He classes tyranny as deviant and leans toward the rule of law over rule by one person, though a uniquely virtuous ruler could justly rule.

state-harmful.rationale: Man is by nature a political animal and the state exists for the good life; the claim that the state is harmful contradicts his foundational thesis.

limit-guns.rationale: Not addressed; no doctrine on arms beyond citizens serving as hoplites, so this is split.

empower-police-military.rationale: He praises military discipline but criticizes Sparta for caring for one part of virtue only, so he would not call for simply more military authority.

legalize-sex-work.rationale: Inferred from state concern for moral formation and temperance; no direct statement.

decide-locally.rationale: The polis is the natural community, favoring local self-government, but he did not address nation-states, and he favors lawgiver-led unity.

rehabilitation.rationale: Laws and punishment are needed to correct passions and form character, supporting both reform and punishment, so adherents are split.

traditional-family.rationale: The household of husband, wife, children and slaves is the first natural community from which the state grows, though the statement concerns family forms he never compared.

same-sex-marriage.rationale: He grounds the household in natural ends of procreation and rule; this inference is low confidence and modern Aristotelians disagree among themselves.

abortion-legal.rationale: Inferred: the Aristotelian natural-law tradition through Aquinas generally opposes legal abortion; Aristotle himself gives no direct position in the sources opened, and modern adherents differ.

heritable-defect-limits.rationale: Inferred: the lawgiver shapes marriage and upbringing for virtue, but state coercion of reproduction is not a stated Aristotelian doctrine in the sources opened and conflicts with household autonomy.

more-religion-public.rationale: The city's gods and cult have a place in the polis, but the Politics gives religion little weight, and later Aristotelians split from Aquinas to secular neo-Aristotelians.

correct-racial-injustice.rationale: Anachronistic; Aristotle's corrective justice and proportional merit give no clear lead, and his own natural-slavery view is a defect adherents often reject.

gender-social-construct.rationale: He holds that natural differences make men lead women in the household, so he would reject the view that gender is primarily constructed.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: He wants education and law to shape citizens to fit their constitution and warns that changing laws weakens habit of obedience, which supports preserving a shared way of life.

gradual-change.rationale: He warns that law has no power to command obedience except habit, so frequent change weakens it; revision is allowed only when a change is clearly better.

reduce-immigration.rationale: He treats resident aliens as non-citizens but gives no immigration doctrine; the question is anachronistic and adherents split.

empower-international-orgs.rationale: The self-sufficient polis is his political unit and he warns against too much unity; inferred opposition to world government.

free-trade.rationale: He regarded commercial exchange for profit as unnatural and wanted a self-sufficient city; free trade is not discussed directly.

nation-first.rationale: No doctrine on nations; the polis seeks its own good life but Aristotle does not rank interests against cooperation.

humanitarian-intervention.rationale: Not addressed; Greek city-states and a theory of just war differ from modern human rights doctrine.

open-borders.rationale: Citizenship is a defined body of persons sharing a constitution, so eventual open borders is a poor fit, though never addressed.

limit-growth.rationale: He wants moderation of wealth and limits on population, but has no environmental concern; the answer is an unresolved inference.

drastic-climate-action.rationale: Anachronistic; his practical wisdom would favor acting on a common good, but no position exists.

tech-solves-problems.rationale: Human flourishing comes from virtuous activity and education, not from technology as such; inferred.

expand-nuclear.rationale: Anachronistic and not derivable from his principles.

revolution-justified.rationale: He analyzes stasis and its causes at length and warns it destroys cities, yet allows that a regime serving only rulers is deviant, so adherents split on revolution.

experts-over-public.rationale: He values practical wisdom, yet argues that the many collectively may judge better than a few experts, though not universally.

central-planning.rationale: He criticizes Plato's enforced unity and communal ownership as destroying the city's plurality, so a command economy would be rejected.

socialized-markets.rationale: Not addressed; he is skeptical of both exchange for profit and common ownership, with no basis for choosing.

land-value-tax.rationale: No fiscal doctrine of this kind; unresolved.

tax-inheritance.rationale: He criticizes land concentration through heiresses and dowries at Sparta, but does not give a doctrine on inheritance tax.

basic-income.rationale: Inferred: the citizen should hold property and take part in the common life, but an unconditional payment is not in his scheme.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: He prefers a self-sufficient city but did not discuss tariffs.

state-directs-investment.rationale: He accepts the lawgiver shaping economic life toward the good, but a doctrine of strategic investment is anachronistic.

widespread-small-property.rationale: His best state has citizens all owning property and a large middle class, and he opposes concentration, though he stresses moderation rather than small ownership as such.

abolish-money-wages.rationale: He treats money as a legitimate invention for exchange and rejects abolition of property, so abolishing money and wages is foreign to his thought.

abolish-central-banks.rationale: Anachronistic; his views on money offer no verdict.

corporatist-bargaining.rationale: He values a common good over class interest but did not propose state-recognized bodies; adherents like Thomist social teaching differ.

one-party-rule.rationale: Rule by the correct constitution is by law for the common good among citizens who share office, and he does not favour a single ideological party.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: Kingship is one of the three correct constitutions, and he says where one family is far superior in virtue it is just that they rule.

democracy-best.rationale: He classes democracy as deviant, though the best of a bad lot and defends the wisdom of the many; the statement says best even when voters choose badly, which he does not endorse.

direct-votes.rationale: He favors mixed constitutions in which the many judge and elect officials, with laws framed by a lawgiver, not direct votes on every law.

workers-councils.rationale: Laborers are excluded from citizenship in his scheme, so workers' councils as the basis of rule is contrary to it.

right-to-secede.rationale: Not addressed; the polis is natural and self-sufficient, but he gives no doctrine on secession.

natural-rulers.rationale: He holds some are naturally suited to rule and others to be ruled, and that a person of outstanding virtue should rule permanently.

political-violence-never.rationale: He warns against faction but never says violence is always wrong; tyrannicide appears in the Politics.

war-builds-character.rationale: He criticizes Sparta for training for war alone and says war serves leisure and peace, not an end in itself.

separate-church-state.rationale: Aquinas-aligned Aristotelians favor cooperation of church and state, and Aristotle's polis has public cult; but there is no developed doctrine.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: Aristotle's law rests on reason and natural ends, not scripture; Thomists add revelation to it, so adherents differ.

private-courts-defense.rationale: Justice and defence are functions of the polis whose citizens deliberate and judge; privatizing them contradicts his view of the state.

military-superiority.rationale: He wants adequate defense but rejects making war the aim of the state; no stance on superiority.

ethnic-nation.rationale: He discusses Greeks and barbarians and a city's suitability, but the nation as ethnic unit isn't his frame.

class-struggle-history.rationale: He sees rich and poor as the source of faction but wants a middle class and mixed regime to prevent it, not conflict as the driver of history.

equal-outcomes.rationale: He says equalizing property misses the problem of desire and favors proportional shares according to contribution to the good life.

civilizational-union.rationale: He warns against excessive unity of the state and builds on the polis; supranational unions are not discussed.

self-interest-moral.rationale: Self-love is acceptable when it aims at virtue but pure self-interested egoism is rejected.

duties-before-rights.rationale: The community is prior to the individual and the good life of citizens is the aim; rights language is anachronistic, but duty of citizens is central.

nature-intrinsic-value.rationale: He views nature teleologically, with plants existing for animals and animals for man, so intrinsic value is not his claim.

limit-population.rationale: He says it is even more necessary to limit population than property, since poverty breeds revolution.

industrial-civilization-disaster.rationale: Anachronistic; his emphasis on flourishing does not condemn industry as such.

accelerate-technology.rationale: Inferred from caution about change and the priority of character.

human-enhancement.rationale: Anachronistic; virtue is acquired by habit, and enhancement is neither endorsed nor excluded.

algorithmic-government.rationale: Practical wisdom is a trained judgment about particulars with no procedure, so replacing it with algorithms is contrary.

unbreakable-encryption.rationale: Encryption is a modern technology Aristotle never considered, and his principles give no lead on privacy against the state.

restore-past-order.rationale: He endorses cautious change and improvement; progress is acceptable when clearly better, so restoring a lost order is not central.

results-over-ideology.rationale: He favors practical wisdom about particulars, but within a framework of virtue and a conception of the good.

direct-action.rationale: He prefers lawful constitutional order and public deliberation, though he does not discuss direct action.

means-match-ends.rationale: Virtue is formed by acting virtuously, so means shape ends; stated of individuals rather than social change.

return-to-foraging.rationale: The polis arises from household and village to enable the good life, which he sees as natural development; a return to foraging reverses that.

abolish-division-of-labor.rationale: His state depends on different roles, such as rulers, ruled and household tasks, with citizens freed for leisure and politics.

distribute-by-need.rationale: Justice is proportional to merit and contribution, not to need alone.

production-for-use.rationale: Natural acquisition is bounded by household need and exchange for profit is unnatural.

profit-exploitation.rationale: He criticizes profit-seeking exchange as unnatural but does not claim profit comes from exploiting workers.

dictatorship-of-proletariat.rationale: Laborers aren't citizens and he condemns rule for a class's advantage as a deviant constitution.

collective-farming.rationale: He argues against common cultivation because disputes arise and people neglect common property.

capitalism-causes-war.rationale: Capitalism and imperialism are modern categories; his concern with unbounded wealth-getting gives no theory of war between powers.

taxation-theft.rationale: The state is natural and may require contributions toward the good life; taxation as theft denies the premise.

harm-principle.rationale: The lawgiver aims at virtue and moral education of citizens, not merely preventing harm to others.

individual-rights-only.rationale: The community is prior to the individual and justice concerns shares in a common life, so his frame is not individual rights.

conscription.rationale: Citizens in the polity are expected to serve as soldiers and share duties; modern conscription is inferred.

exit-over-voice.rationale: Participation in deliberation and office defines citizenship, so exit being more important than voting contradicts that.

state-as-business.rationale: Statecraft aims at virtue and the good life, not profit, and he distinguishes the state from business.

positive-liberty.rationale: Happiness needs external goods and leisure for virtuous activity, so freedom to act virtuously depends on material means, though he never states it as a theory of liberty.

media-academia-power.rationale: Modern media and universities have no counterpart in his writings, so no position can be derived from his principles.

hereditarian-race.rationale: He believed in natural differences between Greeks and barbarians, but the claim about races as genetic ability is not his position and is not endorsed by most modern adherents.

organic-representation.rationale: He sees the polis as composed of households, villages and classes and likes mixed regimes, but never proposes representation by corporate bodies.

total-state.rationale: He rejects Plato's drive for total unity and defends private property and the household, though he accepts state education.

national-rebirth.rationale: He favors cautious reform and moderation over radical rebirth.

territorial-expansion.rationale: He criticizes states that aim at conquest and says war is for the sake of peace and leisure.

personal-loyalty-rule.rationale: Authority rests on law, merit and virtue within a constitution, not on oaths of loyalty.

bound-labor.rationale: He accepts natural slavery and a laboring class without political rights, but not serfdom by that name; modern adherents reject it.

no-neutral-knowledge.rationale: Knowledge, including practical wisdom, aims at truth and the good; a power-based view of truth contradicts it.

universal-morality.rationale: The virtues serve human function and some acts such as murder, theft and adultery are always wrong; practical reason grasps the human good.

single-common-good.rationale: Right constitutions aim at the common advantage and offices go to those who contribute to the good life, rather than balancing interests.

revive-national-language.rationale: Language revival is a modern nationalist question absent from his political thought, with no principle to infer from.

workplace-democracy.rationale: Participation belongs to citizens and not to workers as such; inferred.

school-vouchers.rationale: He says education should be public and not private, as citizens belong to the state.

avoid-deficit-stimulus.rationale: Fiscal stimulus is a modern macroeconomic idea; he wrote nothing on public borrowing or demand management.

economic-freedom.rationale: Political life depends on virtue and moderate property, not on economic freedom; he is critical of unbounded pursuit of wealth.

rule-by-example.rationale: He values moral education and virtuous rulers, but insists on laws and habit to restrain passions.

national-self-determination.rationale: He values the self-governing polis, but nation-based self-determination is anachronistic.

force-without-un.rationale: The UN Security Council is a modern institution, and his thought has no theory of authorizing force between states.

reason-over-faith.rationale: Rational activity in accordance with virtue is the highest human end, but emotion is trained not discarded, and religious Aristotelians add faith, so 'only guide' is too strong.

welfare-for-citizens.rationale: Citizenship is central to his polis but welfare is not discussed.

work-for-welfare.rationale: Welfare schemes and work requirements are not in his writing, and his views on labor and leisure give no clear lead.

class-collaboration.rationale: A large middle class and mixed constitution reduce faction between rich and poor, and the state is a shared community.

sacrifice-heritage.rationale: He advises caution in changing laws and habits that bind citizens.

dominated-front.rationale: Anti-Western fronts are modern geopolitics; nothing in his writings bears on them.

workers-nation.rationale: Workers lack a political role in his framework.

distinct-gender-roles.rationale: He holds that men naturally rule women in the household and that citizens in public life are men.

ban-interest.rationale: He condemns lending at interest as the most unnatural way of getting wealth because money was meant for exchange, not to breed; the statement is about the legal ban, which later Aristotelians such as the scholastics enforced.

racial-segregation-law.rationale: No race-based legal classification in his thought; he distinguishes natural slaves by capacity, not race.

state-class-instrument.rationale: Correct constitutions serve the common good; only deviant ones serve a class, so this is not the state's essence.

expand-fossil-fuels.rationale: Fossil fuel energy policy is wholly modern and not derivable from his principles.

assimilate-immigrants.rationale: Education shapes citizens to the constitution, but immigrants are not discussed.

elite-replacement.rationale: Conspiracy claim with no place in his thought.

proportional-representation.rationale: Not addressed; he favors representing different claims in a mixed constitution.

national-mission.rationale: He rejects conquest as the aim of states; spreading a form of government is not part of his thought.

patriarchy-structural.rationale: He holds male rule in the household is natural, not an unjust structure.

political-elite-corrupt.rationale: He analyzes how deviant regimes serve rulers, but ordinary corruption claims are not his thesis.

security-forces-accountable.rationale: Rule of law counts, but retrospective accountability is not discussed.

night-watchman-state.rationale: The state exists for the good life of citizens and not just security and property.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: He defends natural slavery and the natural rule of men over women, and political rights proportional to virtue, which are contrary to equal worth.

socialism-one-country.rationale: This is an internal Marxist debate, and Aristotle's politics has no stance on socialist strategy.

settler-state-colonial.rationale: Settler colonialism as a category is modern; his remarks on founding cities and conquest give no clear verdict.

uniform-civil-code.rationale: Rule of law counts but he did not discuss religious personal laws.

restrict-conversion.rationale: Conversion between religions was not a political issue in his writings, so no position can be derived.

ban-cattle-slaughter.rationale: Aristotle sees animals as existing for human use; no basis for a ban.

no-religion-state-schools.rationale: He wants education public and virtue-forming, but does not address religious instruction; Thomists differ.

state-strengthens-encirclement.rationale: This is a Marxist-Leninist doctrine about socialist states, and his thought does not address it.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Legitimacy turns on serving the common good and virtue rather than consent; citizens do share in rule, so adherents split.

trade-surplus.rationale: He opposes accumulation for its own sake; mercantilist surplus is inferred opposed.

initiating-force-wrong.rationale: He deems some acts always wrong, but does not hold a non-aggression principle.

competition-drives-progress.rationale: Cooperation in the polis and the good life are central; he views pleonexia as vice.

ban-extremist-parties.rationale: The lawgiver preserves the constitution and he gives advice on preserving regimes, but no doctrine on banning parties.

freedom-as-non-domination.rationale: He says free people rule and are ruled in turn, which is near republican freedom, but he does not theorize it.

separated-powers.rationale: He favors mixed constitutions that blend oligarchic and democratic elements, with deliberative, executive and judicial parts, a forerunner of checks.

vanguard-party.rationale: Rule by a single party for a class contradicts his regime theory.

priority-to-poor.rationale: He wants the poor not to be so poor as to cause faction, but rank priority is not his doctrine.

right-to-buy-council-homes.rationale: Anachronistic, though widespread ownership is approved.

restrict-strikes-picketing.rationale: Strikes and picketing are modern labor-law issues with no counterpart in his writing.

population-causes-poverty.rationale: He says poverty breeds revolution and population must be limited, though he does not rule out institutional causes.

diversity-weakens-cohesion.rationale: He says a city needs plurality but also shared virtue; diversity of ethnicity is not discussed.

offices-by-lottery.rationale: Offices go by merit and contribution to the good life; lottery is characteristic of democracy, which he treats as deviant.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: He accepts law cannot foresee every case and officials fill gaps, but suspension is not discussed.

price-controls-essentials.rationale: He never discusses price ceilings on food in scarcity, and his views on wealth-getting give no firm verdict.

party-controls-media.rationale: He allows the state to control education and music, but no doctrine of a party controlling information.

party-commands-army.rationale: Not part of his regime theory.

long-naturalization-wait.rationale: Citizenship is a status of those who share in office, so inclined to restrict; low inference.

representatives-worker-pay.rationale: Pay for officials is not discussed in the sources opened, and merit-based office does not imply a pay cap.

party-discipline-binding.rationale: Modern political parties did not exist, and his factions are not the same thing, so nothing to infer from.

pool-sovereignty.rationale: He is for the self-sufficient polis and against excessive unity.

head-commands-forces.rationale: Kingship and generalship are discussed, but modern structure is not.

church-by-bishops.rationale: Church governance is outside Aristotle; the question is for Catholic Thomism.

clerical-rule.rationale: The philosopher-ruler is Plato's idea; Aristotle rules by virtue and law, not clergy.

defeat-own-government-war.rationale: Citizens share duties to the polis; a Marxist-style stance contradicts it.

censor-art-for-virtue.rationale: He says music and art shape character through imitation and state education should select them.

unlimited-reelection.rationale: He discusses perpetual office and rotation but not a modern presidency.

recall-officials.rationale: Citizens hold officials to account in the polity, but recall is not discussed.

end-foreign-alliances.rationale: Permanent alliances and overseas troops are modern; his writings on defense give no direct view.

abolish-rental-housing.rationale: He wants moderate property but not abolition of such arrangements.

people-in-arms.rationale: Polity citizens serve as hoplite soldiers, which suggests citizen militias.

rural-life-healthier.rationale: He prefers farming populations as the best citizens in a democracy, and sees retail trade as unnatural; the claim is not moral rural superiority exactly.

reunify-divided-nation.rationale: Nations divided by outside borders are a modern problem not covered in his city-state frame.

educated-out-of-touch.rationale: He values education and practical wisdom; anti-intellectualism is contrary.

cultures-equal-different.rationale: He ranks Greeks above barbarians and holds a universal human good, so judging cultures as only different is contrary.

death-penalty.rationale: He accepts punishment and capital offences in the polis, but never a general doctrine; Thomists accept it.

sex-ed-in-schools.rationale: State education is endorsed, but this content is not addressed.

creationism-in-schools.rationale: His own natural philosophy is teleological but non-creationist, so he would not advocate it.

restrict-pornography.rationale: Laws should protect moral character, and he proposed controlling what young people see and hear.

citizenship-by-descent.rationale: Birth from citizen parents is a common definition he discusses, though he notes it is contested.

minority-language-support.rationale: Language policy for minorities is a modern issue, and his writings are silent on it.

religious-exemptions.rationale: Rule of law and equality before it favor general laws, but not addressed.

encourage-eccentricity.rationale: He values habit, shared education and obedience, and shaping citizens to the constitution.

sovereign-debt-cancellation.rationale: International sovereign debt is modern; he condemned interest but did not address debts between states.

independence-needs-economic-change.rationale: Post-colonial independence is a modern concept, so no position follows from his writings.

constituent-assembly.rationale: He gives a role to the lawgiver, not a constituent assembly; unresolved.

restrict-freedoms-for-growth.rationale: Wealth is instrumental to the good life, not a goal that justifies restricting freedom.

rich-countries-aid-poor.rationale: Beneficence is a virtue, but duties are mainly within communities and friendships.

independent-nuclear-deterrent.rationale: Nuclear weapons are modern and cannot be derived from his theory of defense.

direct-election-head-of-state.rationale: Modes of choosing kings and offices are discussed, but this modern mode is not.

central-bank-independence.rationale: Central banking is a modern institution, and his teaching on money offers no verdict on it.

no-land-for-peace.rationale: This concerns modern territorial disputes with no counterpart in his writing.

property-serves-common-good.rationale: He says property should be 'in a certain sense common' in use, justifying private ownership by its benefit to friends, guests and the city.

soviet-state-capitalist.rationale: This is a Marxist dispute about the Soviet economy that Aristotle's thought does not address.

precautionary-principle.rationale: Practical wisdom might favour caution but there is no direct position.

collective-defense.rationale: Treaty alliances of mutual defense are a modern device, and his writings give no verdict.

annexed-territory-occupation.rationale: The law of occupation and annexation is modern international law, and he gives no view.

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: Aristotle's polis integrates religion; Thomists favour the church's independence, so adherents split.

nonpartisan-head-of-state.rationale: A king rules for the common good, above faction, as in the correct form of kingship.

force-to-prevent-secession.rationale: Secession by regions of a larger state is not addressed in his city-state politics.

region-keeps-system.rationale: Autonomous regions within a larger state are a modern arrangement absent from his thought.

sacred-ruler.rationale: He is hostile to claims of semi-divine kingship except where virtue is god-like; no divine descent claim.

flat-income-tax.rationale: His concept of proportional justice by merit does not map to tax rates.

mixed-constitution.rationale: Aristotle holds that a polity with a numerous middle class is the most stable realistic regime, between oligarchy and democracy.

character-from-environment.rationale: Aristotle holds that virtue comes through habituation and education within the polis, and Politics Book 8 makes public education central, though he also credits nature and reason as sources of character.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: Politics Book 3 argues that law should rule rather than any individual, because law is reason without appetite, and rulers act only where law cannot decide.

space-expansion.rationale: Aristotle's polis is a small self-sufficient community whose size is limited by the good life, so boundless expansion is inferred to be foreign to it.

leader-cult.rationale: Aristotle condemns tyranny and judges rulers by service to the common good, so mass glorification of a leader is inferred to be rejected, though honours for virtue are accepted.

equal-parenting.rationale: Aristotle's household has a hierarchy of father over family; inferred that an equal-time presumption would not follow, and many modern Aristotelians would differ.

class-struggle-under-socialism.rationale: Socialism is not addressed; inferred from Politics II, where Aristotle rejects common property for private property under shared use, so he would doubt both the socialist premise and the claim.

land-redistribution.rationale: Inferred from Politics II, where Aristotle criticises Phaleas's equalisation of land and prefers moderate private holdings, so forced transfer of estates is not his remedy.

refugee-return.rationale: Not addressed; Aristotle ties citizenship to active participation in the polis, but nothing in the sources settles a right of return.

co-ethnic-territorial-claim.rationale: Inferred from the polis ideal of a small self-sufficient community of limited size, which gives no ground for claims over distant co-nationals.

apostasy-punishable.rationale: Not addressed; inferred from his support for civic cult alongside rational inquiry, with no doctrine of punishing a change of belief.

women-must-cover.rationale: No dress law is proposed; Aristotle wants women subordinate in the household, but in Politics II he blames Spartan licence on lax regulation of women only in general terms.

common-currency.rationale: Inferred from his preference for the self-sufficient polis over large unions, which he treats as alliances, not single states.

kin-peoples-union.rationale: Mixed: the polis is the ideal unit, yet he admits larger union is conceivable; the sources do not settle it.

national-cultural-autonomy.rationale: Politics VIII wants one common public education shaping all citizens alike, which leaves little room for separate institutions of a minority.

rights-where-you-live.rationale: Not addressed; Politics III's account of citizenship is about participation in rule and gives no view on minority emigration.

material-conditions-drive-history.rationale: He gives weight to economic causes of faction but holds that ends, virtue and constitutions, not production alone, shape political life.

ban-cartels.rationale: Politics I treats monopoly as a clever but mercenary wealth-getting device, while he also limits unnatural acquisition, so the position is split.

no-bailouts.rationale: Not addressed; inferred from his demand for limited wealth-getting but also moderate property and no rescue scheme.

courts-bound-by-majority.rationale: Politics III holds that law, not the passing will of the many, should rule, and warns that unlimited popular rule becomes tyrannical.

gender-parity-bodies.rationale: Politics I says the male is by nature fitter to command, and he gives women no share in rule, which scope notes records as his position.

economic-self-sufficiency.rationale: Inferred from his emphasis on autarkeia of the polis and on holding imports and foreign dependence limited.

trade-labor-env-standards.rationale: Anachronistic; inferred from his view of the state as shaper of good lives, which cuts both for and against international standards.

moral-incentives.rationale: In the Ethics honour and virtue, not gain, are the proper aims of action and education forms habits of duty, so he would favour moral motives, though he accepts private property.

armed-group-creates-revolution.rationale: Inferred from his analysis of revolutions in Politics V as causes of instability and his preference for mixed constitution and stability.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: Politics III accepts birth and wealth as partial claims to office alongside virtue, so he would not abolish them outright.

history-own-civilization.rationale: Aristotle wants education fitted to the regime and its citizens; inferred that history would be taught from the citizens own polis.

civilizing-tutelage.rationale: Aristotle holds some are natural slaves and that rule over them benefits both; barbarians are placed among those fit to be ruled.

patriotic-education.rationale: Education should be public and fit the constitution so that citizens love their regime.

end-racial-preferences.rationale: Not addressed; Aristotle believed in natural hierarchy but not on racial lines, so no direction can be inferred.

public-money-creation.rationale: Aristotle condemns lending at interest but never addresses money creation; adherents could read this either way.

capitalism-adapts.rationale: Anachronistic; Aristotle did not address capitalist crises.

former-empire-influence.rationale: Not addressed by the doctrine; adherents are split or indifferent, so no direction can be inferred from its principles.

delink-world-market.rationale: Aristotle prizes self-sufficiency but also trade within limits; nothing settles delinking, so this is split.

labor-aristocracy.rationale: Not addressed by the doctrine; adherents are split or indifferent, so no direction can be inferred from its principles.

freedom-to-discriminate.rationale: Law and the community shape character and the good life, so unrestricted private exclusion fits poorly; inferred.

entrenched-bill-of-rights.rationale: Aristotle cautions against changing laws lightly but has no theory of individual rights, so adherents are split.

colonial-treaties-void.rationale: The doctrine does not address this; adherents take varied positions, so it is left neutral.

elective-rulers.rationale: Aristotle accepts election and lot for offices and also kingship where one man excels in virtue, so the answer is split.

minority-veto.rationale: Aristotle treats the collective judgment of the citizen body, by majority, as sovereign in a polity, not a veto for any single member; inferred.

resist-lawless-ruler.rationale: Aristotle classes lawless one-man rule as tyranny, a deviant regime, and holds that law should rule; resistance to a ruler who breaks it fits this.

parliament-supreme.rationale: Law, not any person or body, should be sovereign in Politics III, and he accepts several regime types, so the answer is split.

animal-suffering-matters.rationale: Politics I holds that animals exist for the sake of human use, so their suffering has no independent moral weight.

animal-use-humane.rationale: Politics I endorses using animals for food and clothing; the humane condition is an inference.

noblesse-oblige.rationale: Politics II holds that property should be private but its use common, with the virtue of liberality directing the wealthy to help others.

withdraw-from-politics.rationale: Man is by nature a political animal and the state exists for the good life, so a life withdrawn from public affairs is not the best; though the contemplative life is also prized.

mass-culture-pacifies.rationale: Book 8 holds that music and education shape character to suit the regime, but he treats this as good, not a critique.

ruling-class-consent.rationale: Regimes last when the part of the city that wants them to endure is stronger, and a large middle class steadies them; inferred from the SEP account.

world-economy-extracts-surplus.rationale: The doctrine does not address this; adherents take varied positions, so it is left neutral.

native-born-offices.rationale: Citizenship in Politics III is defined by sharing in office and judgment and is tied to birth from citizens; resident aliens are excluded.

party-own-road.rationale: The doctrine does not address this; adherents take varied positions, so it is left neutral.

self-reliance-over-aid.rationale: The ideal polis is self-sufficient (autarkeia); applying this to foreign aid is an inference.

return-lost-territory.rationale: The doctrine does not address this; adherents take varied positions, so it is left neutral.

indigenous-political-leadership.rationale: The doctrine does not address this; adherents take varied positions, so it is left neutral.

antifascism-founding-value.rationale: Anachronistic; Aristotle opposes tyranny but never addressed this question.

totalitarianisms-equivalent.rationale: Anachronistic; the ideology predates the question and never addressed it.

slavery-not-civil-war-cause.rationale: A historical question outside the ideology.

preserve-contested-monuments.rationale: The doctrine does not address this; adherents take varied positions, so it is left neutral.

male-disadvantage-attention.rationale: The doctrine does not address this; adherents take varied positions, so it is left neutral.

domestic-violence-symmetry.rationale: The doctrine does not address this; adherents take varied positions, so it is left neutral.

institutions-fit-civilization.rationale: Aristotle holds the best regime depends on a people's circumstances and character, and that different peoples suit different constitutions.

military-guardian-role.rationale: Aristotle says those with arms decide a regime's fate, but he does not give the army a guardian role over the constitution.

paid-care-work.rationale: Household management is treated as a natural, non-political sphere, so wage recognition of domestic work is inferred to be rejected.

filial-duty.rationale: Inferred from Aristotle's view of the household as the root of the polis and of reciprocal obligation in the family.

office-by-exam.rationale: Aristotle favours offices going to the virtuous and capable, but through election and selection mixes, not examinations.

foreign-takeover-block.rationale: Not addressed; Aristotle values self-sufficiency but says nothing on foreign ownership of firms.

no-fault-divorce.rationale: Inferred: Aristotle sees marriage as the foundation of household and city, and the Politics does not favour easy dissolution.

recallable-delegates.rationale: Aristotle criticises extreme democracy in which the multitude rules by decree above law, which instructed and recallable delegates resemble.

individual-pension-accounts.rationale: Not addressed; Aristotle treats wealth as instrumental and says nothing on retirement provision.

land-use-tenure.rationale: Aristotle defends private property with common use and criticises Plato's common ownership.

budget-needs-parliament.rationale: Inferred: Aristotle wants officials held to account and public funds controlled by the citizen body.

single-official-language.rationale: Not addressed; Aristotle wants education to shape citizens but is silent on a sole state language.

foreign-land-ownership.rationale: Inferred: Aristotle ties land and citizenship together in the city, so land is for citizens.

disparate-impact-discrimination.rationale: Aristotle's justice is distribution by merit and proportion, not equality of outcomes between groups.

consumerism-harmful.rationale: Wealth-getting beyond need is condemned and wealth is merely a means to the good life.

arm-foreign-insurgents.rationale: Inferred: Aristotle holds war should serve peace and the good life, not subvert other states' regimes.

intervene-in-bloc.rationale: Inferred: Aristotle's states are self-governing polities, with no right of a hegemon to override another's constitution.

corporate-influence.rationale: Inferred from Aristotle's view that regimes ruled by the wealthy for themselves are deviant, so wealth shaping government is a corruption.

restrict-foreign-funding.rationale: Inferred from the polis as a self-sufficient community with a closed citizenship; foreign influence on it is unwelcome.

pronatalist-incentives.rationale: Aristotle favours limits on population size and wealth, so he would not push families to have more children.

residents-only-property.rationale: Inferred from Aristotle's restriction of citizenship to members of the polis and his concern for the polis's stability.

job-guarantee.rationale: Aristotle wants citizens to have leisure for virtue but does not discuss a job guarantee.

democratic-peace.rationale: Aristotle ranks democracy as a deviant form and does not discuss peace between regimes.

no-duty-to-obey.rationale: Law shapes citizens' character and obedience to just law is part of virtue, though unjust law is not owed obedience.

non-intervention.rationale: Not addressed; the Politics has no doctrine of relations between states beyond war for just ends.

industrial-unions.rationale: Not addressed; craft and industrial unions did not exist.

minority-conspiracy.rationale: Inferred from the stress on the common good and a unified citizen body, so groups blamed as plotting enemies of the state do not fit.

abolish-legal-marriage.rationale: Aristotle treats the household and marriage as natural communities that the polis is built on.

public-access-to-information.rationale: Inferred from Aristotle's view that citizens share in deliberation and office, which needs public knowledge of affairs.

local-production.rationale: Book 1 treats the household and the city as aiming at self-sufficiency, which favours local provision.

informal-organisation.rationale: Aristotle sees the constitution and its offices as the ordered form of political life, and treats faction as a danger.

national-law-over-international.rationale: Inferred from the polis having its own constitution and laws with no higher authority above it.

religious-nation.rationale: Aristotle defines the polis by its constitution and citizens' shared pursuit of the good life, not by a religion.

deference-to-leading-power.rationale: Inferred from the Politics' ideal of a self-sufficient polis of free citizens; it prescribes no ritual submission to a leading power.

regional-revenue-retention.rationale: Inferred from the self-sufficient polis ideal, which implies a community keeps and uses its own resources; fiscal federalism is never addressed.

personal-possessions-private.rationale: Aristotle defends private property with common use and criticises Plato's common ownership, though he does not collectivise productive property either.

defeat-communism.rationale: Aristotle criticises Plato's communism but nothing in his thought addresses defeating a rival economic system; adherents would be split.

mixed-public-service-providers.rationale: Inferred from Politics VIII, which makes education a public, state-run concern; delivery by private providers is not discussed.

religion-illusion.rationale: Inferred: Aristotle treats worship and priesthood as a necessary part of the polis, not a consoling illusion, though he never frames religion's origin this way.

capitalism-progressive.rationale: Anachronistic; inferred from his condemnation of unlimited wealth-getting and interest as unnatural, so capitalism as a driver of progress would not be endorsed.

women-equality-needs-economic-change.rationale: Aristotle holds that women are naturally subordinate in the household and polis, so equality is not a goal and economic change is not its route.

socialized-care.rationale: The household is a natural community that exists for daily needs, and Aristotle criticises Plato's common rearing of children as weakening affection.

purge-loanwords.rationale: Inferred: language policy is not addressed, and a theory of natural speech and the polis gives no support for purging words.

treaties-binding.rationale: Inferred from Aristotle's caution about changing established laws and his view that justice includes keeping agreements.

cooperative-communities.rationale: Aristotle rejects communal property and communal households as proposed by Plato, preferring private property with shared use within the polis.

majority-settlement.rationale: Not addressed; Aristotle discusses colonies and faction but nothing settles whether he would favour steered settlement, so this is a split call.

neither-capitalism-nor-communism.rationale: Anachronistic; inferred from his mixed constitution, middle class and private property with common use, a middle path between extremes.

historical-land-claim.rationale: Aristotle ties citizenship and the polis to virtue and the good life, not to a people's ancestral claim on land; inferred.

holocaust-denial.rationale: Not addressed; an adherent would reject denial of established facts, inferred from Aristotle's regard for truth.

criminalize-homosexuality.rationale: Aristotle did not make this a legal question and later Aristotelians split, so adherents are divided.

suppress-opposition.rationale: Aristotle values law and constitutional rule serving the common good, so suppression of all opposition is a mark of deviant regimes; inferred.

punish-blasphemy.rationale: Aristotle treats care of the gods as a first task of the state, so civil punishment of impiety fits, though he does not discuss blasphemy laws; inferred.

colonies-serve-metropole.rationale: Aristotle treats the colony as a city founded for its own good life, not as an economic tool of another; inferred.

defensive-jihad-duty.rationale: Outside the scope; Aristotle did not address Islamic doctrine.

unreligious-rulers-fought.rationale: Aristotle advises caution in changing laws and discusses revolution as a danger, though tyrants may be opposed; inferred.

participatory-democracy.rationale: Citizens share in ruling and being ruled, but Aristotle limits citizenship and prefers a middle-class polity, so this is only a partial fit.

intersecting-oppressions.rationale: Aristotle accepts natural hierarchy of rulers and ruled, including natural slavery and male rule, so adherents of his own view reject this.

gender-identity-recognition.rationale: Anachronistic; Aristotle grounds roles in nature and a fixed human function, so inferred disagreement.

assisted-dying.rationale: Inferred from Aristotle's ethics of courage and the person's duty to the community, which treat taking one's own life as wrong.

left-right-obsolete.rationale: Aristotle's best practical regime is a mixed constitution combining oligarchic and democratic elements, so combining the best of each fits.

alienated-labor.rationale: Aristotle criticises unlimited wealth-getting but also treats manual labour as unfitting for citizens, so adherents would split.

divine-source-of-authority.rationale: Aristotle grounds authority in the state's nature and the common good, not in divine grant; inferred.

religious-dress-in-state.rationale: Not addressed; adherents would be split.

ban-nda-harassment.rationale: Anachronistic; Aristotle values law and justice but never addresses this.

social-market-economy.rationale: Private property with common use, limited wealth-getting and a large middle class point toward a regulated, moderate market; inferred.

abolish-armed-forces.rationale: Aristotle holds that war is for the sake of peace and that a state needs arms for defence, though this is not directly in the sources; inferred.

rich-first.rationale: Aristotle favours a large middle class and moderation of wealth rather than letting some grow far richer first; inferred.

stay-neutral-between-blocs.rationale: Aristotle discusses isolation versus foreign relations but leaves it to circumstance; no clear doctrine.

dynastic-succession.rationale: Politics 3 treats hereditary kingship as problematic because a ruler's children may be unworthy of office, preferring rule by the best.

interest-free-mutual-credit.rationale: Inferred from Aristotle's condemnation of usury as unnatural wealth-getting in Politics 1; he does not discuss mutual banks.

refuse-lender-austerity.rationale: Anachronistic; Aristotle values self-sufficiency but has no position on lender conditions.

property-franchise.rationale: Aristotle's polity and oligarchy give political rights by a property or military-service qualification, and he treats a propertied middle class as the stable core of the citizen body.

domination-women-nature.rationale: Aristotle defends the natural rule of men over women, so he would not accept the premise that ending it is a goal.

reification.rationale: A modern Marxist concept; inferred from Aristotle's view of exchange as a natural convenience whose abuse is moral, not structural.

press-owned-by-wealth.rationale: Inferred from Aristotle's view that the poor lack the leisure and means to take part in politics, so wealth shapes real power.

promulgated-standing-laws.rationale: Politics 3 argues that the law should rule, not any individual, and treats rule by decree as characteristic of the worst form of democracy.

racial-franchise.rationale: Aristotle limits citizenship by birth and status and ranks Greeks above non-Greeks, but his test is citizenship, not race as such.

online-participation.rationale: Anachronistic; inferred from his view that the polis should be small enough for citizens to know one another.

open-government-data.rationale: Inferred from his view that officials should render public accounts of their conduct; he says nothing of open data.

interfaith-marriage-restriction.rationale: Aristotle treats marriage as regulated by the lawgiver for the city's good, but never addresses religious difference.

boycott-minority-shops.rationale: Inferred from his stress on civic friendship as the bond of the city, which targeting a group would damage.

citizens-assembly.rationale: Aristotle notes that selection by lot is characteristic of democracy and mixes lot and election in his best-practicable constitution, but also stresses rule by the qualified, so adherents are split; inferred from Politics Books 3 and 4.

reinterpret-religion.rationale: Aristotle's Politics treats religion as a civic matter and says nothing on reinterpreting religious law; the question is outside the doctrine, so this is a neutral inference.

wealth-concentration-endangers-liberty.rationale: Aristotle holds that extremes of wealth breed faction and tyranny and that a large middle class is the surest basis of a stable regime, though he doubts that equalizing property by law is enough.

open-lgbt-military-service.rationale: Aristotle did not address sexual orientation in military service; adherents split, so this is inferred as neutral.

state-promotes-atheism.rationale: Aristotle makes the cult of the gods a public function of the state and the city, so promoting atheism is inferred to be rejected.

abolish-police-prisons.rationale: Aristotle treats law enforcement and punishment as necessary to the city and its virtue; abolition is inferred to be rejected.

power-sharing-divided-societies.rationale: Aristotle's mixed constitution blends the claims of rich and poor, though it is not about ethnic or religious communities; this is inferred from it.

charity-over-state-aid.rationale: Aristotle holds property should be private but its use shared, with generosity as a virtue exercised through friends; this is inferred to favour private and communal giving over state provision.

term-limits.rationale: Aristotle holds that citizens should rule and be ruled in turn, with offices rotating, which favours limits on how long one person holds office.

vote-delegation.rationale: Aristotle's citizens deliberate and judge in person, and good rule depends on virtue and judgment, so delegable proxy voting is inferred to be disfavoured.

existential-risk-priority.rationale: Aristotle's political thought concerns the good life of the city; extinction risk is outside it, and this is inferred at low confidence.

women-in-religious-leadership.rationale: Aristotle treats women as naturally subordinate in rule and assigns priestly offices to older men; many modern Aristotelians reject this, hence low confidence.

shared-marital-authority.rationale: Politics Book 1 holds that the husband rules the wife as a statesman rules, with the male naturally fitter to command.

missingStatements.text: The best practical constitution mixes rule by the few and the many and relies on a large middle class.
missingStatements.rationale: Aristotle holds that a polity with a numerous middle class is the most stable realistic regime, between oligarchy and democracy.

missingStatements.text: The purpose of the state is to make its citizens virtuous and able to live well, not only to keep them safe and prosperous.
missingStatements.rationale: The state exists for the good life, which is virtuous activity, and the lawgiver's task includes moral education.

notes: Strands differ: Thomist and neo-Aristotelian adherents add religion and reject natural slavery and male rule, so answers on those and on religion are split or low confidence.
